title: Fixed-Size Ring Queue
statement:
Build a first-in, first-out queue that holds at most k values in a fixed block of memory. When the back of the block is used up, new values wrap around into slots freed at the front, so the storage is a ring.

  • RingQueue(k) creates an empty queue with room for k values.
  • enqueue(value) adds a value at the back. Returns true, or false (and changes nothing) if the queue is full.
  • dequeue() removes the front value. Returns true, or false if the queue is empty.
  • front() and rear() return the first and last value, or -1 if the queue is empty.
  • isEmpty() and isFull() report the state.

Every operation should take O(1) time. Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the queue, and the output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: 9 is refused because the queue is full. After 4 leaves, 5 wraps into its freed slot and becomes the rear.
Removing from or peeking into an empty queue fails without an error. One value fills a queue of size 1.

hints: Removing from the front of an array by shifting everything costs O(k). How can you remove without moving any values?
Keep the values where they are and track where the front is with an index. Moving the front means moving that index.
Store head index and count. The back slot is (head + count) mod k. Enqueue writes there; dequeue advances head = (head + 1) mod k. Full is count = k, empty is count = 0.

explain.intuition:
A queue built on Array.prototype.shift moves every remaining value one slot left on each dequeue. A ring buffer never moves values. It keeps a fixed array of k slots, an index head pointing at the front value, and a count. The rear slot is (head + count − 1) mod k, and the modulo is what makes the array wrap around like a ring.

Keeping a count rather than only two indexes avoids the classic ambiguity where head === tail could mean either empty or full. Ring buffers are everywhere in frontend and systems code: audio buffers in Web Audio, log tails, and the last-N-frames history in a performance overlay.
steps: enqueue(v): if count === k return false. Write buf[(head + count) % k] = v, increase count, return true.
dequeue(): if count === 0 return false. Set head = (head + 1) % k, decrease count, return true.
front() is buf[head] and rear() is buf[(head + count − 1) % k], both -1 when empty.
pitfalls: Using only head and tail with no count: head === tail is both the empty and the full state. Either keep a count or waste one slot.
Computing the rear as tail − 1 without wrapping. When tail is 0, the rear is slot k − 1, not −1.
Returning a stale value from front() after everything was dequeued. Check for empty first.

solutions.title: Plain array with shift
solutions.idea: Push to the back and shift from the front. Correct, but each dequeue moves every remaining value.

solutions.title: Ring buffer with head and count
solutions.idea: A fixed array plus a head index and a count. The back slot is found with modulo, so nothing ever moves.

followups: Make it a double-ended queue: add and remove at both ends in O(1). What changes in the index arithmetic?
One thread only enqueues and another only dequeues. Why can a ring buffer then work without a lock?
